transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Uh… mostly, people keep telling me I’m not listening. Like my supervisor, or my wife, they’ll be talking right to me, and then a minute later I realize I only got part of it. Then I have to ask them to repeat themselves. It’s been causing problems.
When people say you're not listening, is it because you literally can't hear or understand what they're saying clearly, or do you hear them fine but your mind seems to wander or drift elsewhere?
I hear them fine. It’s more like… they’re talking right to me, and then I realize I only caught part of it. Then I have to ask them to say it again.
Would you say this trouble focusing and missing parts of conversations has been happening since you were a kid, or is this something that started more recently, like in the past several months?

Yeah… it goes way back. I was like that as a kid too. Teachers were always moving my seat because I couldn’t stay put, and I’d call out answers or get in trouble for butting into other kids’ work. That was before middle school, I think.
Right now, are these attention problems causing noticeable difficulties in more than one area of your life—like both at work and at home—or is it mainly in just one setting?

It’s more than one place, yeah. Work’s gotten pretty serious… I’ve had formal warnings, and I worry I could mess something up on the line. At home, my wife and kids get frustrated too, because I kind of disrupt the routine instead of helping.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since childhood, prior to middle school) pattern of inattentive symptoms (missing parts of conversations, needing repetition, distractibility despite normal hearing/comprehension) combined with a childhood history of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (couldn't stay seated, teachers repositioned him, called out answers, interrupted others). Symptoms have persisted into adulthood and currently cause clinically significant impairment across multiple settings—occupational (formal warnings, safety concerns at work) and domestic (marital/family friction, disruption of routines). This combination of chronic inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms with childhood onset and cross-situational impairment meets criteria for ADHD, predominantly inattentive-currently-presenting picture but with historical combined features, coded as F90.0.
